proposal.utterance: Classify 'Abusus' (the right of abuse, in Roman-law property theory) in BFO terms.

entities.label: Abusus
entities.rationale: Abusus is the right of disposal or alienation that inheres in an owner with respect to a thing. In Roman law property theory it is one of the three standard incidents of dominium (usus, fructus, abusus). As a legal incident it is a normatively conferred, externally grounded capacity assigned to a bearer (the owner) by the legal system—paradigmatically a Role under BFO_0000023. It is already a subtype of LegalRight (which is typed as BFO_0000023), so subclassing under LegalRight is the most precise placement. It is modeled as a class (kind) because 'Abusus' denotes a type of right rather than any particular instance.

relations.rationale: Abusus is a specific species of LegalRight (a right of disposal/alienation), itself typed as BFO_0000023 (Role), capturing that it is an externally grounded legal incident inhering in an owner-bearer.

open_questions: Should Abusus be further distinguished from usus and fructus by minting sibling classes (Usus, Fructus) under LegalRight to represent the full tripartite Roman dominium structure?

Is Abusus being requested as a general class (the kind of right), or does the user want a specific historical instance—e.g., the Abusus right as recognised under classical Roman law in a particular period?

Should a class 'Dominium' (or 'PropertyRight') be minted as an intermediate parent between LegalRight and Abusus, with Usus and Fructus as siblings, to model the mereological structure of Roman property rights?
Roman Abusus includes both alienation inter vivos and testamentary disposition—should these be modelled as sub-roles or as distinct realisable entities?
proposal.rationale_summary: Abusus, the Roman-law right of disposal, is classified as a class (kind) typed as BFO_0000023 (Role) via subclassing the existing working:LegalRight class. The Role typing is appropriate because Abusus is a normatively conferred, externally grounded legal incident that inheres in the bearer (the dominus/owner) in virtue of the legal system's recognition of ownership—not an intrinsic disposition of the person. BFO Roles inhere in their bearers (RO_0000052) and are realised in processes (BFO_0000054); correspondingly, Abusus would be realised in acts of alienation, sale, gift, or destruction. Placing it under working:LegalRight captures that it is a right-type rather than an obligation or bare authority, consistent with how LegalRight is already modelled. No individuals are introduced because the utterance requests classification of the kind, not a specific token instance.
